key_terms.meaning: Energy that travels through space as oscillating electric and magnetic fields, carrying information from a target to a sensor
Distance between two consecutive crests of the wave, measured in metres or micrometres (1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m)
Number of wave cycles passing a point per second, in hertz; f = c ÷ λ, where c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light
Energy of one quantum of radiation, E<sub>p</sub> = h f = h c ÷ λ, with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s; in eV, E<sub>p</sub> = 1.24 ÷ λ(µm)
λ<sub>max</sub> = 2898 ÷ T (µm, kelvin): the sun peaks at 0.50 µm, the earth at 9.7 µm
A wavelength band where the atmosphere absorbs very little, so a sensor placed there can see the ground
Scattering by gas molecules much smaller than λ, varying as 1 ÷ λ⁴; it makes the clear sky blue
Ratio of reflected radiant flux to incident flux at a surface, a pure number from 0 to 1, often written as a percentage
Radiant flux leaving a unit area into a unit solid angle, in W·m⁻²·sr⁻¹; what the sensor actually measures
Light scattered into the sensor's view by the atmosphere; ρ = π (L − L<sub>p</sub>) ÷ (T E)
The curve of reflectance against wavelength for a surface; its shape identifies the material
The steep rise in vegetation reflectance between about 0.68 μm and 0.75 μm, caused by leaf cell structure
Normalised Difference Vegetation Index = (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> − ρ<sub>red</sub>) ÷ (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> + ρ<sub>red</sub>); values run −1 to +1 (dense crop about 0.8, soil about 0.1, water negative)
A near-polar orbit at about 700–900 km whose plane keeps a fixed angle to the sun, so each pass crosses at the same local time
Sensor with a linear array of detectors that images a whole line of ground at once as the platform moves forward
Sensor that supplies its own energy and records the return, e.g. radar or LiDAR; it works day or night
T = 2π √(a³ ÷ μ), a = R + h, μ = 398 600 km³/s²: 98.9 min at 705 km, one sidereal day at 35 786 km
Ground distance covered by one pixel, in metres; smaller value means finer detail
Number of discrete brightness levels a sensor can record, e.g. 8 bits gives 2⁸ = 256 levels
Time between two images of the same ground point, also called the repeat cycle; measured in days
Relative brightness or darkness of a feature on an image; the most basic interpretation clue
Reading a feature from its neighbours, e.g. a small white rectangle beside a road is probably a building
S = f ÷ (H − h) for a vertical photo; area scale is the square of the linear scale
Image built by putting near-infrared in red, red in green and green in blue; healthy vegetation appears bright red
Assigning pixels to classes after training the computer on sample areas of known class chosen by the analyst
κ = (p<sub>o</sub> − p<sub>e</sub>) ÷ (1 − p<sub>e</sub>): agreement beyond chance in an error matrix

takeaways: Every remote sensing measurement begins with electromagnetic energy, and wavelength alone fixes both the frequency and the photon energy.
Between the sun and the sensor the atmosphere scatters and absorbs energy, so the sensor records radiance that has been altered twice.
The atmosphere is transparent only in certain windows, which is why sensors are built for specific wavelength bands.
Reflectance is a property of the surface; radiance is what reaches the sensor, and the two differ by atmospheric effects and illumination geometry.
Vegetation, soil and water each have a distinct reflectance-versus-wavelength curve, and the differences between the curves allow identification.
A remote sensing system is a platform plus a sensor; orbit choice fixes repeat time and viewing geometry, and sensor geometry fixes image shape.
The four resolutions limit what an image can show, and improving one usually costs another.
Visual interpretation combines tone, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow and association with site knowledge before any software is used.
Digital processing turns raw digital numbers into corrected, enhanced images and then into labelled classes, with an accuracy table to judge the labels.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to run in one line from electromagnetic radiation and its interaction with the atmosphere and target, through sensors, platforms and the four resolutions, to visual interpretation and digital classification, using spectral signature curves as the connecting thread.

bank.q: Explain the wave and particle models of electromagnetic radiation. Show how wavelength fixes frequency and photon energy, and name the spectral regions used in optical remote sensing with their approximate wavelength ranges.
outline: Oscillating electric and magnetic fields at right angles, travelling at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
f = c ÷ λ and E<sub>p</sub> = h f = h c ÷ λ, with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s
Inverse relation: longer wavelength means lower frequency and lower photon energy
Regions: visible 0.4–0.7 µm, near infrared 0.7–1.3 µm, short-wave infrared 1.3–3 µm, thermal infrared 8–14 µm, microwave 1 mm–1 m
Wave model explains reflection, refraction, diffraction and polarisation; particle model explains absorption, emission and detection
Why band choice follows the physics: Wien peaks, thermal bands detect emission, microwave penetrates cloud

answer.text: Wave model. Electromagnetic radiation (EMR) is an electric field and a magnetic field oscillating at right angles to each other and to the direction of travel. In vacuum, and very nearly in air, it travels at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Wavelength λ is the distance between crests; frequency f is the number of crests passing a point each second. They are tied by c = f λ.

Particle model. EMR also arrives as photons, packets of energy E<sub>p</sub> = h f = h c ÷ λ, with h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s. In electron volts this is E<sub>p</sub> = 1.24 ÷ λ, with λ in µm (1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).

Worked values. Green light, λ = 0.55 µm = 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ m: f = 3 × 10⁸ ÷ 5.5 × 10⁻⁷ = 5.45 × 10¹⁴ Hz; E<sub>p</sub> = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5.45 × 10¹⁴ = 3.61 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.26 eV. The same working across the spectrum:

Inverse relation. Because c is fixed, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency and a lower photon energy: the 10 µm photon carries 0.124 ÷ 2.26 = 1/18 of the green photon's energy. Photon energy is not beam power; a warm surface emits very many weak infrared photons.

Regions used in optical remote sensing: visible 0.4–0.7 µm (eye, true colour), near infrared 0.7–1.3 µm (vegetation), short-wave infrared 1.3–3 µm (moisture, minerals), mid infrared 3–8 µm with a usable window at 3–5 µm (fires), thermal infrared 8–14 µm (surface temperature). Microwave, 1 mm to 1 m, is used by radar and radiometers.

Which model explains what. The wave model explains reflection, refraction, diffraction, polarisation and the phase that radar interferometry uses. The particle model explains absorption and emission by molecules (a gas absorbs only photons whose energy matches its transitions) and how a detector converts photons to an electrical signal.

Why band choice follows the physics. Wien's law λ<sub>max</sub> = 2898 ÷ T puts the sun's peak (5800 K) at 0.50 µm, so reflected-light sensors work at 0.4–2.5 µm, and the earth's peak (300 K) at 9.66 µm, so thermal sensors work at 8–14 µm and can image at night. Microwave photons pass through cloud, so radar works in the monsoon.

bank.q: Describe how the atmosphere modifies incoming and outgoing electromagnetic radiation. Explain Rayleigh, Mie and non-selective scattering, absorption, and the idea of atmospheric windows.
outline: Scattering and absorption act on the downward solar path and again on the upward path to the sensor
Rayleigh: particles much smaller than λ, intensity varies as 1 ÷ λ⁴, strong in blue, causes haze
Mie: aerosols about the size of λ (dust, smoke, sea salt), weakly wavelength dependent, forward-peaked, grey-white urban haze
Non-selective: particles much larger than λ (water droplets, cloud), scatters all visible wavelengths equally, gives white cloud
Absorption by ozone, carbon dioxide and water vapour in specific bands
Atmospheric windows: visible, 0.8–1.3, 1.5–1.8, 2.0–2.4, 3–5 and 8–14 µm, and microwave
Effect on image: reduced contrast, bluish haze, need for atmospheric correction

answer.text: Two passes. Sunlight crosses the atmosphere on the way down to the ground and the reflected light crosses it again on the way up to the sensor. On both passes the atmosphere scatters and absorbs, and on the way up it also adds path radiance L<sub>p</sub>, light scattered into the sensor's view that never touched the ground.

Rayleigh scattering is caused by gas molecules (N₂, O₂) much smaller than the wavelength. Its strength varies as 1 ÷ λ⁴. Blue at 0.45 µm is scattered (0.70 ÷ 0.45)⁴ = 5.86 times more than red at 0.70 µm and (0.85 ÷ 0.45)⁴ = 12.7 times more than near infrared at 0.85 µm. Hence the blue sky, the red low sun, and haze that is worst in blue bands.

Mie scattering is caused by aerosols about the size of the wavelength (0.1 µm to a few µm): dust, smoke, sea salt, pollen. It depends only weakly on wavelength, is strongest in the forward direction and gives the grey-white veil over a city.

Non-selective scattering is caused by particles much larger than the wavelength, such as cloud droplets and coarse dust. All visible and near-infrared wavelengths scatter about equally, so cloud and fog look white and hide the ground in every optical band.

Absorption turns radiation into heat at wavelengths matching molecular transitions: water vapour near 1.4, 1.9 and 2.7 µm; carbon dioxide near 2.7 and 4.3 µm and beyond 14 µm; ozone in the ultraviolet and near 9.6 µm; oxygen in narrow bands near 0.69 and 0.76 µm.
Atmospheric windows are the gaps between absorption bands where most energy gets through. Every sensor band is placed in one:

Effect on the image, with numbers. Take a field of reflectance 0.157 under E = 400 W/m², upward transmittance T = 0.9 and path radiance L<sub>p</sub> = 4.0 W m⁻² sr⁻¹. It leaves the ground at ρE ÷ π = 20.0, reaches the sensor as 0.9 × 20.0 + 4.0 = 22.0, and gives an uncorrected reflectance π × 22.0 ÷ 400 = 0.173. Haze lifts dark pixels, flattens contrast and biases reflectance upwards, so atmospheric correction is needed before comparing dates.
Check. Corrected: π (22.0 − 4.0) ÷ (0.9 × 400) = 56.55 ÷ 360 = 0.157, the true value; and the blue-to-red Rayleigh ratio 5.86 agrees with 0.70⁴ ÷ 0.45⁴ = 0.2401 ÷ 0.0410 = 5.86.

bank.q: Draw and explain the spectral reflectance curves of healthy vegetation, dry soil and clear water over the visible to shortwave infrared range. State how the curves are used to identify these surfaces.
outline: Vegetation: chlorophyll absorption in blue and red, small green peak near 0.55 μm, red edge at 0.68–0.75 μm, high near-infrared plateau from leaf cell structure, water absorption dips near 1.4 and 1.9 μm
Soil: smooth, gradually rising curve, no sharp features; brightness depends on moisture, organic matter, iron, texture
Water: low reflectance in visible, falls further into near-infrared; turbid water rises in visible; clear water almost black in near-infrared
Snow: very high reflectance in visible, drops in shortwave infrared
Curve shape as a signature; band ratios separate the surfaces
Physical reasons behind each feature, not just shape

svg.aria: Reflectance curves of vegetation, dry soil and clear water from 0.4 to 2.5 micrometres, with the red and near-infrared bands shaded.

answer.text: Healthy vegetation. Chlorophyll absorbs blue (0.45 µm) and red (0.67 µm), so reflectance is about 5% there, with a small green peak of about 12% at 0.55 µm. At the red edge, 0.68–0.75 µm, reflectance rises steeply to a near-infrared plateau of 45–50%, because light scatters inside the leaf between cell walls and air spaces. Beyond 1.3 µm leaf water absorbs, giving dips near 1.4 and 1.9 µm and about 30% at 1.6 µm and 18% at 2.2 µm.

Dry soil. A smooth curve rising slowly from about 10% at 0.45 µm to 18% at 0.66 µm, 22% at 0.83 µm and about 33% at 2.2 µm, without pigment features. Moisture lowers the whole curve and deepens the water dips; organic matter darkens it; iron oxides raise red; fine texture brightens it.

Clear water. Highest in blue (8–9%), falling through green and red (4% at 0.66 µm) to almost zero in near infrared (2% at 0.83 µm) and beyond, because water absorbs infrared strongly. Turbid water is brighter in the visible, especially red; algae add a green peak.
Snow is very bright in the visible (often above 80%) and drops sharply in the short-wave infrared, where ice absorbs; that drop separates snow from cloud.
Using the curves. A sensor samples each curve in a few bands. The red and NIR values below, read from the sketch, give NDVI = (NIR − red) ÷ (NIR + red):

Identification rules from the shapes: a large NIR-to-red jump means vegetation; a gentle rise with no jump means soil; reflectance falling to near zero in NIR means water; bright visible with a short-wave infrared drop means snow. The physical cause of each feature (pigment, cell structure, water, minerals) is what the examiner wants with the shape.
Check. The three NDVI values are in the right order and range: vegetation near +1 side (0.818), soil just above zero (0.100), water negative (−0.333), all within −1 to +1.

bank.q: Classify remote sensing platforms and sensors. Explain passive and active sensors, geostationary and sun-synchronous orbits, and the difference between whiskbroom and pushbroom scanning.
outline: Platforms: ground-based, airborne (aircraft, UAV), spaceborne (satellite, space station)
Passive sensors use reflected or emitted natural radiation; active sensors carry their own transmitter, e.g. radar, LiDAR
Geostationary orbit: 35 786 km above the equator, period one sidereal day, fixed view, coarse resolution, continuous monitoring
Sun-synchronous near-polar orbit at about 700–900 km, fixed local solar time, global coverage, repeat cycle of days
Whiskbroom: one or a few detectors per band with a moving mirror scanning across track; short dwell time limits radiometric precision
Pushbroom: linear detector array images a full line, longer dwell time, no moving mirror, geometric distortions differ
Examples of sensor types: panchromatic, multispectral, hyperspectral, thermal, SAR, LiDAR

answer.text: Platforms by height:

head: Platform
Height
Use
rows: a few hundred metres to 10 km
site mapping on demand, disaster response
repeated wide coverage, national mapping, weather

answer.text: Passive and active sensors. A passive sensor records natural energy: reflected sunlight (multispectral cameras, needs daylight and clear sky) or emitted heat (thermal scanners, work at night) or natural microwave emission (radiometers). An active sensor carries its own transmitter and records the echo: SAR uses microwaves and sees through cloud day and night; LiDAR uses laser pulses to measure range.

Sun-synchronous orbit. Near-polar, inclination about 98°, height usually 600–900 km. Its plane turns about 1° a day eastwards, keeping pace with the earth's motion round the sun, so it crosses each latitude at the same local solar time and sun angles match between dates. At 705 km: T = 2π √(7083³ ÷ 398 600) = 5933 s = 98.9 min, 14.56 orbits a day, successive tracks 2752 km apart at the equator, so full coverage takes days (16 for Landsat 8).

Geostationary orbit. Circular, over the equator, at 35 786 km: T = 2π √(42 164³ ÷ 398 600) = 86 164 s, one sidereal day, so the satellite stays over one longitude and views the same hemisphere continuously. Pixels are coarse (about 0.5–4 km) because of the distance; it suits weather and cyclone watch.

Whiskbroom scanning. A mirror sweeps one detector (or a few per band) across the track while the platform moves along it; each image line is built pixel by pixel. It needs moving parts and gives each pixel a very short dwell time.

Pushbroom scanning. A fixed line of detectors across the track images a whole line at once; forward motion adds the next line. No mirror, and each detector dwells on its pixel for the whole line time.

Dwell time with numbers. At 600 km the ground track speed is 6.91 km/s. For a 10 m pixel a pushbroom detector dwells 10 ÷ 6908 = 1.45 ms. A whiskbroom with one detector must cover all 6000 pixels of the line in that time: 1.45 ms ÷ 6000 = 0.24 µs per pixel, 6000 times less light collected, which is why pushbroom images have better signal-to-noise.

Sensor types: panchromatic (one wide band, fine detail), multispectral (a few bands), hyperspectral (hundreds of narrow bands), thermal, SAR, LiDAR. Indian examples: Resourcesat (multispectral, sun-synchronous), Cartosat (high-resolution panchromatic), RISAT (SAR), INSAT (geostationary weather).
Check. The geostationary period 86 164 s is 23 h 56 min, one turn of the earth relative to the stars; the dwell-time ratio 1.45 ms ÷ 0.24 µs = 6000, the number of detectors.

bank.q: Explain the four resolutions of a remote sensing image with suitable examples, and describe the trade-offs between them.
outline: Spatial resolution: ground size of one pixel, in metres; 5.8 m on one well-known Indian imaging satellite versus 10 m to 30 m on open missions
Spectral resolution: number, width and placement of bands; panchromatic single wide band versus hyperspectral with hundreds of narrow bands
Radiometric resolution: bits per pixel, 8 bits gives 256 levels, 11 bits gives 2048 levels
Temporal resolution: repeat cycle in days; geostationary gives minutes, polar orbiting gives days, some high-resolution sensors can be tasked
Trade-offs: finer spatial resolution usually means narrower swath and longer repeat; more bands mean lower signal per band
Application-driven choice

answer.text: Spatial resolution is the ground size of one pixel side, the ground sampling distance GSD = H θ for a detector angle θ. A sensor at 700 km with θ = 10 µrad gives 700 000 × 10 × 10⁻⁶ = 7 m. Example values: 5.8 m on one well-known Indian multispectral camera, 10 m to 30 m on free open missions. Smaller numbers are finer.
Mixed pixels follow from it: nine 10 m pixels with DNs 10, 10, 10, 10, 70, 70, 10, 70, 70 become one 30 m pixel of 330 ÷ 9 = 36.7 → 37, a value of neither cover.

Spectral resolution is the number, width and position of bands. Panchromatic: one wide band (about 0.5–0.75 µm). Multispectral: four to a dozen bands, such as red 0.63–0.69 and NIR 0.76–0.90 µm. Hyperspectral: contiguous narrow bands; 10 nm bands from 0.4 to 2.5 µm give (2.5 − 0.4) ÷ 0.01 = 210 bands.

Radiometric resolution is the number of levels, 2ⁿ for n bits: 8 bits give 256 (DN 0–255), 11 bits 2048, 12 bits 4096. For a band spanning 0–120 W m⁻² sr⁻¹ µm⁻¹ the step is 120 ÷ 255 = 0.471 at 8 bits but 120 ÷ 4095 = 0.0293 at 12 bits, so two fields 0.20 apart share DN 128 at 8 bits and read 2049 and 2056 at 12 bits.

Temporal resolution is the revisit time. A geostationary imager repeats every few minutes; a sun-synchronous satellite at 705 km with a 185 km swath repeats its track every 16 days; pointable high-resolution satellites and constellations revisit in a day or two.
Trade-offs:

head: Improve
Cost
rows: narrower swath for the same detector count (6000 detectors: 10 m → 60 km swath, 5 m → 30 km), so longer revisit
less energy per band, lower signal-to-noise
more data: a 12-bit band is 1.5 times an 8-bit band
wide swath and coarse pixels, or many satellites

answer.text: Application-driven choice: crop monitoring wants red and NIR at 10–30 m every few days; urban mapping wants 1–5 m pixels and can wait longer; flood and cyclone watch want revisit in hours, so geostationary or SAR.

bank.q: A vegetation index image is to be prepared from a sensor whose red band is 0.63–0.69 μm and near-infrared band is 0.76–0.90 μm. Compute NDVI at two pixels: pixel A with red reflectance 0.05 and near-infrared reflectance 0.45; pixel B with red 0.20 and near-infrared 0.30. Interpret both values and state two limitations of NDVI.
outline: Formula: NDVI = (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> − ρ<sub>red</sub>) ÷ (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> + ρ<sub>red</sub>)
Pixel A: (0.45 − 0.05) ÷ (0.45 + 0.05) = 0.40 ÷ 0.50 = 0.80, dense healthy vegetation
Pixel B: (0.30 − 0.20) ÷ (0.30 + 0.20) = 0.10 ÷ 0.50 = 0.20, sparse or stressed cover, or mixed soil
Range check −1 to +1; water gives negative values, thick cloud and bare rock values near zero
Limitations: saturates over dense canopy, affected by soil background and atmosphere, needs red and near-infrared bands
Why the ratio reduces illumination differences

answer.text: Formula. NDVI = (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> − ρ<sub>red</sub>) ÷ (ρ<sub>NIR</sub> + ρ<sub>red</sub>), with reflectances as fractions. The red band (0.63–0.69 µm) sits on chlorophyll absorption; the NIR band (0.76–0.90 µm) sits on the leaf's bright plateau, past the red edge.

Interpretation. A (0.80) is dense, healthy green vegetation: very low red because chlorophyll absorbs it, high NIR from leaf structure. B (0.20) is sparse or stressed vegetation, or a pixel mixing crop and soil; bare dry soil sits near 0.1, water below zero. B could also be a paddy field just after transplanting, where water and wet soil still show between the young seedlings.

Why a ratio. If a slope receives only 60% of the light, A becomes red 0.03 and NIR 0.27: NDVI = 0.24 ÷ 0.30 = 0.80, unchanged. Dividing by the sum cancels a common brightness factor that a single band cannot.
Range check. NDVI lies between −1 and +1: water gives negative values (more red than NIR), thick cloud, snow-free rock and bare soil give values near zero to 0.2, crops 0.3–0.9.

Limitations (any two, explained): (1) it saturates over dense canopy, so a crop at leaf area index 4 and one at 6 may both read about 0.85–0.9; (2) bright or wet soil showing between plants shifts the value, which is why the soil-adjusted SAVI exists; (3) haze adds path radiance mainly in red and lowers NDVI unless the image is corrected; (4) different sensors' band widths give slightly different NDVI for the same field.

Reading values on a map. Common rough classes are: below 0, water; 0 to 0.2, bare soil, rock or built-up; 0.2 to 0.5, sparse or stressed vegetation; above 0.5, dense green vegetation. They are guides, not fixed limits, because they shift with sensor bands, season and soil.
Check. Recompute B from its definition with percentages: (30 − 20) ÷ (30 + 20) = 10 ÷ 50 = 0.20, the same as with fractions, so the scale of the numbers does not matter.

bank.q: An image of 8000 columns by 8000 rows is recorded at 11-bit radiometric resolution in four bands. Calculate the number of grey levels, the raw storage in megabytes, and the ground area covered if the pixel size is 5.8 m. Comment on how storage changes if the data are stored as 8-bit.
outline: 11 bits gives 2¹¹ = 2048 grey levels
Total pixels = 8000 × 8000 = 6.4 × 10⁷
Bits = 6.4 × 10⁷ × 11 × 4 = 2.816 × 10⁹ bits, divide by 8 for bytes and by 10⁶ for megabytes ≈ 352 MB
At 8 bits: 6.4 × 10⁷ × 1 × 4 bytes = 2.56 × 10⁸ bytes ≈ 256 MB
Ground area = 6.4 × 10⁷ × (5.8)² m² ≈ 2.15 × 10⁹ m² ≈ 2153 km²
Comment: fewer bits save space but quantise brightness and may lose detail in dark targets

answer.text: Grey levels. 11 bits give 2¹¹ = 2048 levels, DN 0 to 2047.
Pixels per band. 8000 × 8000 = 6.4 × 10⁷.
Raw bits. 6.4 × 10⁷ pixels × 11 bits × 4 bands = 2.816 × 10⁹ bits.
In practice 11-bit values are stored in 16-bit (2-byte) words, so the file is 6.4 × 10⁷ × 4 × 2 = 5.12 × 10⁸ bytes = 512 MB unless the bits are packed.
Ground area. One pixel covers 5.8 m × 5.8 m = 33.64 m². The scene covers 6.4 × 10⁷ × 33.64 = 2.153 × 10⁹ m² = 2153 km², a square of 8000 × 5.8 m = 46.4 km on a side (46.4² = 2153).
As 8-bit data: 6.4 × 10⁷ × 4 bands × 1 byte = 2.56 × 10⁸ bytes = 256 MB, that is 8 ÷ 11 = 73% of the packed 11-bit size and half the 16-bit file.

Comment. Rescaling 2048 levels to 256 merges every 8 levels into one, so brightness differences smaller than 8 of the original steps disappear. The loss matters most in dark targets (water, shadow, dense forest), where the useful signal spans only a few dozen of the 2048 levels; for display only, 8 bits is enough, for quantitative work keep the 11-bit data. A common compromise is to archive the 11-bit master and make a stretched 8-bit copy for viewing and sharing.

Transfer time, for scale. Over a 100 Mbit/s link the packed 11-bit scene (2.816 × 10⁹ bits) takes 2.816 × 10⁹ ÷ 10⁸ = 28.2 s and the 8-bit scene (2.048 × 10⁹ bits) 20.5 s, so cutting bits also cuts download and archive cost in the same 8 : 11 proportion.

bank.q: You must monitor paddy crop growth every week over a district of about 5000 km². Choose the platform type, orbit, band set and resolution, and justify each choice. Then state how you would convert the images into a crop-area map.
outline: Platform: spaceborne, since the area is large and weekly coverage is needed
Orbit: sun-synchronous polar, fixed local time for comparable illumination; swath wide enough to cover the district in one or two passes
Bands: red and near-infrared for NDVI, plus shortwave infrared for moisture; possibly green for visual composites
Spatial resolution: 10 m to 30 m adequate for field-level crop mapping; finer resolution increases data volume without need
Temporal resolution: repeat cycle of about 5 days or better, or a constellation, to get cloud-free weekly observations
Processing: geometric and atmospheric correction, NDVI time series, supervised classification on training fields, accuracy check on ground truth
Mention cloud cover as the main operational risk in the monsoon

answer.text: Platform: spaceborne. 5000 km² every week is far beyond aircraft or drone surveys, and a satellite repeats the same view at no extra effort.

Orbit: sun-synchronous, so every image is taken at the same local time and sun angle and NDVI values are comparable across weeks. A swath of 100–300 km covers a district of about 70 km × 70 km in one or two passes.

Bands: red and NIR for NDVI and crop vigour, short-wave infrared (about 1.6 µm) for water in the flooded fields and crop moisture, green for composites. Because paddy grows in the monsoon (kharif), add a C-band SAR sensor: optical images are often cloudy. If each optical pass is clear with probability 0.4 and two passes fall in a 10-day window, the chance of no clear image is 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36; SAR sees through the cloud, and flooded paddy (dark, smooth water) stands out from growing rice.

Spatial resolution: 10–30 m. Data per band: 5000 km² at 10 m is 5000 × 10⁶ ÷ 100 = 5 × 10⁷ pixels; at 30 m it is 5.6 × 10⁶. A typical 0.5 ha (5000 m²) paddy plot holds 50 pixels at 10 m but only 5.6 at 30 m, so 10 m is the better choice for small holdings; finer than 5 m adds data without improving the crop map.
Temporal resolution: a revisit of 5 days or better, from one satellite or a constellation, to get at least one usable look per week; SAR fills the cloudy weeks.

Processing to a crop-area map: (1) geometric correction to the map grid with control points; (2) atmospheric correction to reflectance, or calibration of SAR backscatter; (3) a cloud mask; (4) an NDVI time series for every pixel through transplanting, tillering and heading; (5) supervised classification using training fields visited on the ground; (6) area = number of paddy pixels × pixel area (100 m² at 10 m); (7) accuracy check with an error matrix at independent test fields.

Main risk: monsoon cloud, handled by combining SAR with optical data. Secondary risks: mixed pixels on bunds, and other crops with a similar NDVI at the same date, handled by using the full time series.
Check. If 1.2 × 10⁷ pixels at 10 m are classified as paddy, the area is 1.2 × 10⁷ × 100 m² = 1.2 × 10⁹ m² = 1200 km², 24% of the 5000 km² district, a plausible figure.

bank.q: A raw image has digital numbers between 40 and 120 in an 8-bit file. Explain how a linear contrast stretch, a histogram equalisation and a band ratio would each change the image, and state which you would use to bring out a faint drainage pattern and why.
outline: Raw data occupy a narrow part of the 0–255 range, so the image looks flat and dark
Linear stretch maps input minimum and maximum to 0 and 255, output = (DN − min) × 255 ÷ (max − min); preserves relative brightness
Histogram equalisation redistributes values so each grey level is equally frequent; boosts local contrast but changes relative brightness
Band ratio divides one band by another, cancelling illumination differences and highlighting absorption features
For faint drainage: contrast stretch first, since the pattern is a tonal and textural feature and relative brightness matters; histogram equalisation may amplify noise
Principal component analysis and edge enhancement as further options

answer.text: The raw image uses DN 40 to 120 out of 0–255, about 80 ÷ 255 = 31% of the display range, so it looks flat and grey.
Linear contrast stretch: DN(out) = (DN(in) − 40) ÷ (120 − 40) × 255 = 3.19 × (DN(in) − 40).

It keeps the order and the relative spacing of brightness: a faint stream at DN 62 on a background of 66, 4 levels apart, becomes 70 against 83, 13 levels apart, which the eye can see. Values outside 40–120 (if a tighter min and max are chosen) are clipped.

Histogram equalisation reassigns values so that each output level holds about the same number of pixels; output = 255 × the cumulative fraction of pixels up to that input DN. If 40% of the pixels lie between 60 and 70, that 10-level slice is spread over about 0.40 × 255 = 102 output levels. Busy DN ranges gain contrast and rare ranges lose it; relative brightness is no longer kept and noise in uniform areas is amplified.

Band ratio divides one band by another pixel by pixel, for example NIR ÷ red. A common illumination factor cancels: a sunlit field (0.40 ÷ 0.08 = 5.0) and the same field in shade (0.20 ÷ 0.04 = 5.0) give the same ratio. It brings out material differences such as vegetation, moisture or iron-bearing soil, and suppresses the relief shading that often outlines drainage.

Choice for a faint drainage pattern: the linear stretch, possibly followed by an edge-enhancing high-pass filter. Drainage shows as narrow lines of slightly different tone and as the shading of valley sides; the stretch enlarges those small tone differences while keeping their order, and an edge filter sharpens the lines. Equalisation may lift noise to the same level as the streams, and a ratio would cancel the shading that marks the valleys.
Further options: principal components (the first component gathers the shared brightness and texture), a directional edge filter along the expected flow direction.
Check. The stretch sends the ends correctly: (40 − 40) × 3.19 = 0 and (120 − 40) × 3.19 = 255; the 4-level gap becomes 4 × 3.19 = 12.75 ≈ 13 levels.

bank.q: A sensor at altitude records radiance, but the analyst wants surface reflectance. Analyse the factors that separate the two, and evaluate how atmospheric correction and ground reference data improve the estimate.
outline: Radiance is at-sensor flux per unit area per unit solid angle; reflectance is a surface property
Path radiance from scattering adds a constant bias; absorption removes signal in some bands
Illumination geometry: solar zenith and azimuth angle, topographic slope and aspect change the incident flux
Adjacency effect and mixed pixels from finite sensor footprint
Correction methods: dark object subtraction, radiative transfer models, empirical line calibration against bright and dark targets
Residual error remains; indices such as NDVI and band ratios reduce but do not remove it
Evaluate: relative correction is enough for classification, absolute reflectance needed for multi-date quantitative work

answer.text: Definitions. Radiance L is the power per unit area per unit solid angle arriving at the sensor, in W m⁻² sr⁻¹; it depends on the sun, the atmosphere and the view. Reflectance ρ is the fraction of incoming light the surface returns, a property of the ground alone.

The link for a Lambertian surface: L = T ρ E ÷ π + L<sub>p</sub>, so ρ = π (L − L<sub>p</sub>) ÷ (T E), where E is the irradiance at the ground, T the upward transmittance and L<sub>p</sub> the path radiance.

Factors that separate them: (1) path radiance from Rayleigh and Mie scattering, an additive bias largest in blue; (2) absorption by water vapour, ozone and CO₂, which removes signal in some bands; (3) illumination: E = E<sub>0</sub> cos θ<sub>z</sub>, so the same field receives cos 30° = 0.866 of the overhead value at a 30° solar zenith angle but only cos 60° = 0.50 at 60°; slope and aspect change the local angle further; (4) sensor calibration: DNs must first be turned into radiance with the gain and offset; (5) adjacency and mixed pixels, where light from neighbouring bright surfaces spills in.

Worked case. E = 400 W/m², T = 0.9, L<sub>p</sub> = 4.0. A field reading L = 22.0 gives an uncorrected ρ = π × 22.0 ÷ 400 = 0.173 and a corrected ρ = π × 18.0 ÷ 360 = 0.157: the error is 10% of the true value.

Dark object subtraction: the darkest pixels in a band (deep clear water, deep shadow) should have reflectance near zero, so their radiance is taken as L<sub>p</sub>. If the darkest water reads 4.0, subtract 4.0 from the whole band. Simple and image-based, but it ignores T and assumes a truly dark object exists.

Empirical line with ground reference data: measure two targets in the field with a spectrometer, a dark one (ρ = 0.05) and a bright one (ρ = 0.45), and read their image radiance, here 9.73 and 55.57. A straight line through them: slope = (55.57 − 9.73) ÷ (0.45 − 0.05) = 114.6, intercept = 9.73 − 114.6 × 0.05 = 4.0. The field then gives ρ = (22.0 − 4.0) ÷ 114.6 = 0.157. The ground data fix both T E ÷ π (the slope) and L<sub>p</sub> (the intercept) at once.
Radiative transfer models (6S, MODTRAN) compute T and L<sub>p</sub> from the sun and view angles and the aerosol and water-vapour amounts; they need no ground targets but need good atmospheric data.

Evaluation. For a single-date classification a relative correction (or none) is often enough, because all classes are shifted alike. For multi-date change detection or for physical quantities (NDVI trends, water quality, albedo) absolute surface reflectance is needed, and ground reference targets are the best check. Indices and ratios reduce, but do not remove, illumination and haze effects.
Check. The empirical line reproduces the model: 114.6 = T E ÷ π = 0.9 × 400 ÷ 3.1416 = 114.6, and the intercept 4.0 equals L<sub>p</sub>.

bank.q: Compare visual image interpretation with digital classification for mapping land use. Evaluate when a trained interpreter still beats software, and how the two can be combined.
outline: Visual: uses tone, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow, site and association; needs experience and site knowledge; slow over large areas; reproducible only with effort
Digital: uses pixel values and statistics; fast, repeatable, handles many bands; needs training data and ground truth; suffers from mixed pixels and spectral confusion
Visual wins on shape and context reasoning, e.g. separating a road from a canal of the same tone, and on small areas with fine detail
Digital wins on large areas, multi-band and multi-date data, and quantitative indices
Hybrid: digital classification aided by on-screen visual editing, image segmentation into objects then classification
Accuracy assessment by confusion matrix, overall accuracy and kappa coefficient

answer.text: Visual interpretation uses the elements tone or colour, shape, size, pattern, texture, shadow, site and association, checked against an interpretation key and in the field. It needs a trained interpreter and local knowledge; it is slow over large areas and two interpreters may draw different boundaries.

Digital classification uses the DNs of several bands and their statistics. Supervised methods (maximum likelihood, random forest) learn from training areas; unsupervised methods (k-means) find clusters that the analyst names. It is fast and repeatable and handles many bands and dates, but it confuses covers with similar spectra and labels mixed pixels badly.
Comparison:

head: Point
Visual
Digital
rows: pixel values, a few derived features

answer.text: Where the interpreter still wins: separating covers of the same tone by shape and context (a canal from a road of the same grey, a building roof from a dry field, a stadium identified by its car park); small areas at very fine resolution; old panchromatic photos with one band; and judging whether a change is real or seasonal.
Where software wins: large areas, many bands and dates, quantitative indices (NDVI time series), and maps that must be repeated each season the same way.

Measuring both by the same yardstick. In the error matrix of the worked classification (300 test pixels) overall accuracy is 249 ÷ 300 = 0.830 and κ = (0.830 − 0.382) ÷ (1 − 0.382) = 0.725. The weak cell is 27 built-up pixels mapped as crop, a confusion an interpreter often fixes by pattern (rows of roofs) and association (roads).

Combining the two: use visual keys to choose training areas; classify digitally; edit doubtful patches on screen; segment the image into objects and classify the objects with shape and texture as well as spectra (object-based analysis); check both with the same error matrix.
Evaluation. Neither replaces the other: digital classification gives the speed and repeatability, the interpreter gives context and judgement. The hybrid gives the best accuracy per hour of work.
Check. p<sub>e</sub> = (50 × 52 + 150 × 140 + 100 × 108) ÷ 90 000 = 0.382, and κ = 0.448 ÷ 0.618 = 0.725, lower than 0.830 as kappa always is when chance agreement is positive.

bank.q: Two images of the same coastal city, five years apart, are to be used to map urban growth. Analyse the requirements on resolution, registration and season, and evaluate the sources of error in the resulting change map.
outline: Requirements: same or similar sensor and bands, similar spatial resolution, images from the same season and near-same time of day to match sun angle and phenology
Accurate geometric registration to within a fraction of a pixel, otherwise edges produce false change
Radiometric normalisation between dates, since sensor gain and atmosphere differ
Methods: image differencing, band ratio, principal component analysis, post-classification comparison
Errors: misregistration, mixed pixels along boundaries, phenology and tide differences, cloud and shadow, classification error propagating into the change map
Evaluate: post-classification comparison gives a clear change matrix but doubles the classification error; differencing is more sensitive but harder to label
Validate with high-resolution imagery or field check

answer.text: Sensor and bands. Use the same or a closely matched sensor on both dates, with the same bands (at least red, NIR and short-wave infrared, which separate concrete, soil and vegetation) and a similar pixel size; resample the finer image to the coarser grid if they differ.

Season and time. Choose both images from the same season and near the same local time, so crop stage, tree leaf, sun angle and shadow length match. On a coast, also check the tide level, because a wider beach or a filled creek can look like new land.

Registration. The two images must overlay to a fraction of a pixel. A half-pixel shift at 30 m is 15 m; along a city edge 40 km long that shift creates a false-change band 15 m × 40 000 m = 6 × 10⁵ m² = 0.6 km², enough to hide real growth of the same size.
Radiometric normalisation. Convert both images to reflectance, or match them with targets that did not change (deep water, old runways), because sensor gain, haze and sun angle differ between dates.

Methods: image differencing (subtract the band or NDVI values), band ratio, change in principal components, or post-classification comparison (classify each date, then cross the two maps into a from-to change matrix). In NDVI differencing, a pixel that falls from 0.6 (crop) to 0.1 (roofs and roads) changes by −0.5 and passes a threshold of −0.3, so it is flagged as new built-up; a seasonal fall from 0.6 to 0.45 (−0.15) is not.

Error sources: misregistration; mixed pixels along boundaries; seasonal and tidal differences; cloud and shadow on one date; and classification errors that add up. If each date's map is 85% correct and errors are independent, a pixel is right on both maps with probability 0.85 × 0.85 = 0.72, so the change map is only about 72% reliable.

Evaluation. Post-classification comparison gives a clear from-to table (crop to built-up, water to built-up) and tolerates different sensors, but compounds the errors of two maps. Differencing is more sensitive to small changes and uses one threshold, but its results are harder to label and it needs very good normalisation. Validate the change map with high-resolution imagery or a field check at sample points.
Check. 15 m is half of 30 m; 0.85² = 0.7225; 0.6 km² = 600 000 m² = 667 pixels of 900 m².

bank.q: A newly designed satellite must serve both agriculture monitoring and urban mapping. Evaluate how the choice of orbit, swath, band set and spatial resolution constrains each other, and propose a reasonable design with justification.
outline: Sun-synchronous polar orbit gives a fixed local time, useful for both applications, with a repeat cycle of a few days
Narrow swath gives fine pixels but long revisit; wide swath gives frequent coverage but coarse pixels
Agriculture needs red and near-infrared for vegetation indices and frequent revisit, moderate resolution is acceptable
Urban mapping needs fine spatial resolution and panchromatic sharpening, but that pushes data volume and cost up
Design compromise: multispectral at moderate resolution plus a panchromatic band, off-nadir tasking for rapid revisit
Signal-to-noise falls as pixels shrink; radiometric resolution must be adequate
Conclusion: state the trade-off explicitly and defend the chosen numbers

answer.text: Orbit. Sun-synchronous near-polar at about 705 km: T = 98.9 min, 14.56 orbits a day, track spacing 2752 km at the equator, fixed local time (about 10:30) so both applications get comparable sun angles.
Swath and pixel are tied by the detector count: swath = pixels across × pixel size. With 12 000 detectors, 2.5 m pixels give a 30 km swath; with 6000 detectors, 10 m pixels give 60 km.

Revisit from the swath alone: to fill 2752 km between neighbouring tracks a 30 km swath needs about 2752 ÷ 30 = 92 days and a 60 km swath about 46 days, far too long for crops. Pointing the camera ±25° across track at 705 km reaches 705 × tan 25° = 329 km either side, so a chosen site can be seen every few days without changing the orbit.

Agriculture needs red and NIR (NDVI), green and short-wave infrared, at 10–20 m, every 5 days or better; urban mapping needs 1–3 m detail, which a panchromatic band gives, and can accept a longer revisit.

Data rate. Line rate = ground speed ÷ pixel: 6755 ÷ 2.5 = 2702 lines/s for pan and 675 lines/s at 10 m. Pan: 12 000 × 12 bits × 2702 = 389 Mbit/s. Multispectral: 6000 × 4 bands × 12 bits × 675 = 195 Mbit/s. Both exceed what one ground station can take continuously, so the satellite images selected areas or compresses the data.

Signal-to-noise. A 2.5 m pixel collects (10 ÷ 2.5)² = 16 times less light than a 10 m pixel in the same exposure time, so the panchromatic band is made wide (about 0.5–0.75 µm) to gather enough energy; radiometric resolution of 11–12 bits keeps dark urban shadows and water usable.
Proposed design:

head: Item
Choice
Reason
rows: 4 bands (green, red, NIR, SWIR) at 10 m, 60 km swath
two satellites, 180° apart in the same orbit

answer.text: Conclusion. The choice is a trade-off stated in numbers: finer pixels cost swath, revisit, signal and data rate. Splitting the mission into a moderate-resolution multispectral camera for crops and a pointable panchromatic camera for cities serves both users.

glossary.def: Transfer of radiation energy into a medium, such as a gas molecule or a leaf, so that it is not returned to the sensor.
Fraction of incident solar radiation reflected by a surface over all wavelengths, a single broadband number.
A wavelength interval where absorption is weak, allowing the sensor to see the ground.
A narrow wavelength interval recorded as one image channel by a sensor.
Point operation that maps a narrow range of digital numbers onto the full display range to improve visibility.
Whole number stored for each pixel of a band; it is related to radiance by the sensor's calibration gain and offset.
Radiation given out by a body because of its temperature, described by Planck's law.
Image made by assigning three different wavelength bands to red, green and blue display channels; colours are not natural.
Circular equatorial orbit at about 36,000 km altitude where the satellite keeps pace with Earth's rotation and appears fixed.
Angular cone seen by one detector at one instant; its projection on the ground sets the pixel size.
Measure of classification agreement after removing the agreement expected by chance alone.
Active system that sends laser pulses and times the return to measure distance and build a three-dimensional surface model.
The point on the ground directly below the sensor; the viewing direction straight down.
One picture element, the smallest cell of a raster image, holding a single digital number per band.
Radiant flux per unit projected area per unit solid angle reaching the sensor, in W·m⁻²·sr⁻¹.
Dimensionless ratio of reflected to incident flux at a surface, ranging from 0 to 1.
Synthetic Aperture Radar, an active microwave sensor that uses platform motion to build a fine-resolution image and sees through cloud.
Ratio of image distance to corresponding ground distance, e.g. 1:25,000.
Redirection of radiation by particles or molecules without absorption, producing haze and path radiance.
Ground width covered by the sensor in one sweep or one pass.
Frequency of tonal change in a group of pixels, giving a rough or smooth appearance used in visual interpretation.
Fraction of incident radiation that passes through a medium, the complement of absorption and scattering losses.
Grouping pixels into statistically similar clusters without training samples, after which the analyst names the clusters.
Sensor that sweeps one detector, or a few per band, across the track with a moving mirror while the platform moves forward.
Radiance scattered into the sensor's line of sight by the atmosphere without touching the ground; it brightens hazy images.
Table of mapped classes against reference classes at test pixels; it gives overall, user's and producer's accuracy and kappa.
The peak wavelength of a blackbody is 2898 ÷ T µm, with T in kelvin.
